question: God shaped the first man from the dust of the ground, breathed life into him, and set him in a garden called Eden to tend it. What was the man's name?
context: The story is in Genesis 2. Adam means 'man' or 'from the earth' in Hebrew. God formed Eve from one of Adam's ribs while he slept and brought her to him as his companion.

question: A serpent in the Garden of Eden tempted the first woman to eat from the one tree God had forbidden — the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. What was the woman's name?
context: The story is in Genesis 3. Adam ate from the fruit Eve offered him. God expelled them from Eden and placed cherubim with a flaming sword to guard the way back. Eve means 'mother of all the living.'

question: Two brothers brought offerings to God — one of crops, one of a lamb. God favored the shepherd's lamb. The jealous farmer killed his brother in a field. Who killed his brother Abel?
context: The story is in Genesis 4. Cain was marked by God and exiled east of Eden to the land of Nod. When God asked where Abel was, Cain replied: 'Am I my brother's keeper?'

question: God warned Noah that a flood would cover the earth and told him to build a huge wooden ark and load it with two of every animal. How long did the rain fall?
context: The story is in Genesis 6-9. After the flood, God set a rainbow in the sky as a promise never to destroy the earth by water again. Noah's three sons (Shem, Ham, Japheth) repopulated the earth.

question: After the flood, Noah sent a bird out from the ark three times to see if dry land had appeared. The third time the bird returned with an olive leaf in its beak. What kind of bird was it?
context: The story is in Genesis 8. Noah first sent a raven that did not return. The dove returned the second time with the olive leaf, then the third time did not return at all — Noah knew the land was dry.

question: After the flood, all the people of earth spoke one language and tried to build a tower reaching to heaven. God confused their speech so they could not understand each other. What was the tower called?
context: The story is in Genesis 11. The name Babel sounds like the Hebrew word for 'confused.' The scattering of languages from Babel explains the origin of the world's different tongues.

question: God called an old shepherd named Abraham to leave his country and travel to a new land God would show him. He promised Abraham's descendants would be as numerous as what?
context: The story is in Genesis 12-15. God also compared Abraham's descendants to the sand on the seashore. Abraham is called the father of three faiths — Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

question: God tested Abraham by ordering him to sacrifice his only son on Mount Moriah. As Abraham raised the knife, an angel stopped him and a ram was provided instead. What was the son's name?
context: The story is in Genesis 22. The ram was caught by its horns in a thicket. Christians have long read the binding of Isaac as a foreshadowing of God offering His own Son. The story is sacred to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam alike.

question: God planned to destroy two wicked cities. He warned Lot and his family to flee and never look back. Lot's wife glanced back and was turned to a pillar of what?
context: The story is in Genesis 19. The cities were Sodom and Gomorrah. Fire and sulfur rained down on them. A salt formation by the Dead Sea is still called 'Lot's Wife' by locals.

question: Jacob's favorite son was given a special coat of many colors that made his brothers jealous. They threw him into a pit and sold him to traders going to Egypt. What was the son's name?
context: The story is in Genesis 37. Joseph was the eleventh of Jacob's twelve sons but the firstborn of his beloved wife Rachel. He had dreamed that the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him.

question: A Hebrew shepherd was tending his father-in-law's flock on Mount Horeb when he saw a bush on fire that was not burning up. From the bush, God spoke his name. Who was the shepherd?
context: The story is in Exodus 3. God told Moses to take off his sandals because he stood on holy ground. Moses asked God's name and was told 'I AM WHO I AM' — Yahweh in Hebrew.

question: When Pharaoh refused to free the Hebrew slaves, God sent ten plagues on Egypt — frogs, locusts, darkness, and more. What was the very last plague?
choices: A rain of fire from heaven
context: The story is in Exodus 7-12. The Hebrews marked their doorposts with lamb's blood so the angel of death would pass over them. The Passover festival commemorates this. Pharaoh's own firstborn son died that night.

question: Pharaoh's chariots chased the Hebrews to the Red Sea. Moses raised his staff. The sea parted and they crossed dry. What befell the Egyptians?
answer: The waters crashed back and drowned them
choices: The waters crashed back and drowned them
They fled back to Egypt in great fear
An angel struck them blind on the sand
context: The story is in Exodus 14. Miriam, Moses's sister, led the Hebrew women in a song of victory with tambourines. The crossing is celebrated in Jewish tradition every Passover.

question: On Mount Sinai, surrounded by thunder and fire, God gave Moses two stone tablets. What did the tablets contain?
choices: The names of the twelve tribes
A map to the Promised Land
context: The story is in Exodus 19-20. The first tablet covered duties to God; the second, duties to neighbors. Moses smashed the first set when he found the people worshipping a golden calf. God gave him a second set to replace them.

question: While Moses was on Sinai, the Hebrews grew impatient and melted their gold jewelry. They built and worshipped an idol shaped like an animal. What did they make?
context: The story is in Exodus 32. Moses came down the mountain, smashed the tablets in rage, ground the calf to powder, mixed it in water, and made the people drink it. Three thousand were killed for the idolatry.

question: Joshua led the Hebrews to Jericho. For six days they marched silently around it. On the seventh day they marched seven times and blew rams' horns. What happened?
choices: Fire fell from heaven on it
context: The story is in Joshua 6. The Hebrews then took the city, sparing only Rahab — a woman who had hidden Israelite spies in her house, marked by a scarlet cord in her window.

question: An Israelite judge had supernatural strength as long as his hair was never cut. His Philistine wife Delilah tricked him into revealing his secret and cut his hair while he slept. Who was he?
context: The story is in Judges 13-16. The Philistines blinded Samson and set him to grind grain in prison. His hair grew back, and at a feast he pulled down the temple of Dagon, killing himself and thousands of Philistines.

question: A young woman from Moab refused to leave her widowed mother-in-law and followed her back to Bethlehem. She gleaned grain in the field of a rich kinsman who eventually married her. Who was she?
context: The story is in the Book of Ruth. The kinsman was Boaz. Their great-grandson was King David. Ruth's loyal vow to Naomi — 'Whither thou goest, I will go' — remains one of the most quoted lines in scripture.

question: A Jewish queen of Persia risked her life by going uninvited before the king to expose the plot of an evil minister named Haman, who planned to kill all Jews. What was the queen's name?
context: The story is in the Book of Esther. Haman had built a fifty-cubit gallows to hang Esther's cousin Mordecai — but Haman was hanged on it himself. The Jewish festival of Purim celebrates the rescue.

question: A nine-foot Philistine giant named Goliath dared Israel's army to send one champion to fight him. A shepherd boy stepped out with only a sling and five smooth stones. Who was the boy?
context: The story is in 1 Samuel 17. The stone struck Goliath's forehead and the boy then used the giant's own sword to cut off his head. David later became Israel's greatest king and ancestor of Jesus.

question: Two women claimed the same baby. King Solomon ordered the baby cut in half — knowing the true mother would beg him to spare the child even if it meant giving it up. What was Solomon famous for?
context: The story is in 1 Kings 3. Solomon was the son of David and Bathsheba. He built the great Temple in Jerusalem. He had asked God for wisdom rather than riches, and so God gave him both.

question: King David saw a beautiful woman bathing on a rooftop and arranged for her husband to be killed in battle so he could marry her. What was the woman's name?
context: The story is in 2 Samuel 11-12. The prophet Nathan confronted David with the parable of the poor man's lamb. David repented. Bathsheba and David's son was Solomon, who built the Temple.

question: An Old Testament prophet challenged the priests of Baal to call down fire on their altar. They failed; he soaked his own altar with water and called on the Lord — and fire fell. Who was the prophet?
context: The story is in 1 Kings 18. The contest happened on Mount Carmel. King Ahab and Queen Jezebel had been promoting Baal worship. After the fire, Elijah had all the prophets of Baal slaughtered at the Kishon brook.

question: At the end of his life, the prophet Elijah did not die — God took him up to heaven in something burning, drawn by horses of fire. What carried Elijah up?
context: The story is in 2 Kings 2. The prophet Elisha watched it happen and inherited Elijah's cloak — and a double portion of his spirit. The 1981 film *Chariots of Fire* takes its title from this scene.

question: King Darius signed a decree that no one could pray to any god but the king for thirty days. A Hebrew official kept praying toward Jerusalem and was thrown to the lions. Who was he?
context: The story is in Daniel 6. The next morning the king found Daniel alive — an angel had shut the lions' mouths. The conspiring officials who had reported Daniel were then thrown into the den with their families.

question: A Hebrew prophet ran from God's command and boarded a ship. A great storm rose and the sailors threw him overboard. A huge fish swallowed him and he prayed inside it for three days. Who was he?
context: The story is in the Book of Jonah. The fish spat him out on dry land. Jonah then went to Nineveh as commanded and preached, and the whole pagan city repented in sackcloth and ashes.

question: An angel appeared to a young woman in Nazareth named Mary, telling her she would have a son and name him Jesus. The angel said the Holy Spirit would come upon her. What was the angel's name?
context: The story is in Luke 1. Mary's response — 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word' — is called her Fiat. The visit is called the Annunciation; it is celebrated on March 25.

question: Mary and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem because of a Roman census. There was no room at the inn, so Mary gave birth to Jesus and laid him in a what?
answer: A manger (a feeding trough for animals)
choices: A manger (a feeding trough for animals)
A cradle in the innkeeper's loft
A wooden basket beside the door
A bed of straw on the temple floor
context: The story is in Luke 2. The Gospels do not specify a stable, but the manger implies a place where animals were kept. The town was Bethlehem, where King David had also been born — fulfilling the prophecy of Micah.

question: On the night Jesus was born, an angel appeared to humble field workers and the sky filled with a heavenly host singing. Who were the workers?
context: The story is in Luke 2. The angels sang 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.' The shepherds left their flocks at once to go and see the baby in the manger.

question: Wise men from the East followed a star to Bethlehem to find the newborn king. They brought him three gifts. Two were gold and frankincense. What was the third?
context: The story is in Matthew 2. The wise men (or Magi) are traditionally named Caspar, Melchior, and Balthazar. Gold honored a king, frankincense honored a priest, and myrrh — a burial spice — foreshadowed Jesus's death.

question: King Herod, hearing of a newborn 'king of the Jews,' ordered all male children in Bethlehem under age two to be killed. An angel warned Joseph in a dream to flee with Mary and Jesus. Where did they go?
context: The story is in Matthew 2. The killing is called the Massacre of the Innocents. The Holy Family stayed in Egypt until Herod died, then returned to Nazareth. The flight is the subject of countless medieval paintings.

question: A wild-living preacher in the wilderness wore camel-hair clothes and ate locusts and wild honey. He baptized people in the River Jordan, including Jesus. Who was he?
context: The story is in Matthew 3. John was Jesus's older cousin. When Jesus came up from the water, the heavens opened, the Spirit descended like a dove, and a voice said: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'

question: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers casting nets — Simon and Andrew. He called them to follow him. What did he say they would now catch instead of fish?
context: The story is in Matthew 4. Jesus told them: 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.' Simon's name was later changed to Peter — meaning 'rock' in Greek — and he became the chief apostle.

question: Jesus chose twelve close followers to be his apostles. They included Peter, Andrew, James, John, and a tax collector named Matthew. Including Judas Iscariot, how many were there?
context: The twelve apostles match the twelve tribes of Israel. After Judas's betrayal and death, the remaining eleven cast lots and chose Matthias to replace him. Paul is sometimes called the thirteenth apostle.

question: At a wedding in Cana the wine ran out. Mary asked Jesus to help. He told servants to fill six stone jars with water. When the steward tasted what came out, what was it?
answer: The finest wine of the feast
choices: The finest wine of the feast
A red juice of crushed grapes
Cold milk of the temple goat
context: The story is in John 2. This was Jesus's first public miracle. The steward marveled to the bridegroom: 'You have kept the good wine until now.' Each jar held twenty or thirty gallons.

question: Five thousand followed Jesus into the wilderness with nothing to eat. A boy offered all he had brought. Jesus blessed it and fed them all. What did the boy have?
answer: Five loaves of bread and two fish
choices: Five loaves of bread and two fish
Three cakes and a jar of honey
A wineskin and a basket of dates
context: The story is the only miracle (other than the Resurrection) recorded in all four Gospels. Twelve baskets of leftover scraps were gathered. The boy's basket is called a *kophinos* in Greek — a small lunch basket.

question: Caught in a storm at night on the Sea of Galilee, the disciples saw Jesus coming toward their boat. He was not swimming or rowing — he was doing something else. What?
choices: Borne on the waves by angels
context: The story is in Matthew 14. Peter asked to come out and walk too. He began to sink when he doubted, and Jesus caught him: 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' When they got into the boat the wind ceased.

question: Caught in a sudden storm on the Sea of Galilee, the disciples woke Jesus, who was asleep in the boat. He stood up and rebuked the wind and waves. What happened?
choices: The storm grew twice as fierce
An angel appeared and steered the boat
The boat lifted from the water to the shore
context: The story is in Mark 4. The disciples whispered to each other: 'What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' Jesus had said only three words: 'Peace, be still.'

question: Jesus heard that his friend Lazarus had died and his sisters Mary and Martha were mourning. Jesus stood at the tomb and cried out a name. What did the dead man do?
answer: Walked out of the tomb alive
choices: Walked out of the tomb alive
Sat up but could not speak
Vanished from the tomb in light
context: The story is in John 11. Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Jesus wept before the miracle — the shortest verse in the Bible. Lazarus came out still wrapped in grave-cloths; Jesus said: 'Loose him, and let him go.'

question: Jesus told a story about a man beaten by robbers and left for dead on the road. Two religious men passed by. Only an unexpected traveler stopped to help. Who was that traveler?
context: The story is in Luke 10 — the parable of the Good Samaritan. Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Jesus turned a question about 'who is my neighbor?' into an answer about who showed mercy. The Samaritan paid the innkeeper to nurse the man.

question: A father's younger son demanded his inheritance, wasted it in a far country, and ended up feeding pigs. He came home expecting nothing. What did the father do?
answer: Ran to him and threw a great feast
choices: Ran to him and threw a great feast
Sent the servants to drive him off
Made him work to repay the debts
context: The story is in Luke 15 — the parable of the Prodigal Son. The father killed the fatted calf. The elder son resented the welcome. Jesus told it to show how God receives sinners who return.

question: Jesus told of a shepherd with a hundred sheep. One wandered off. The shepherd left the ninety-nine and searched until he found it. Why?
choices: Because the lost one was the best
context: The story is in Luke 15 — the parable of the Lost Sheep. The shepherd carried the sheep home on his shoulders and called his neighbors to celebrate. Jesus said: 'There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.'

question: Jesus described the kingdom of heaven as starting from the smallest of all seeds. When planted, it grows into a tree so large that the birds come and nest in its branches. What seed?
context: The parable is in Matthew 13. Jesus also said that faith as small as a mustard seed could move mountains. The actual black mustard plant of the Holy Land can grow to ten feet — a tree from a tiny seed.

question: On a mountainside in Galilee, Jesus preached his most famous sermon. It begins with the Beatitudes — 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful…' What is this sermon called?
context: The Sermon on the Mount is in Matthew 5-7. It includes the Lord's Prayer, the Golden Rule, and the command to love your enemies. Augustine called it 'the perfect standard of the Christian life.'

question: On the night before his death, Jesus shared a Passover meal with his twelve disciples in an upper room in Jerusalem. He broke bread and gave them wine. What is this meal called?
context: Jesus took the bread and said: 'This is my body.' He took the cup and said: 'This is my blood of the new covenant.' Christians remember the meal in the Eucharist (Communion). Leonardo da Vinci painted the most famous image of it.

question: One of the twelve disciples agreed to betray Jesus to the chief priests. He led them to the Garden of Gethsemane and identified Jesus with a kiss. Who was he?
context: Judas accepted thirty pieces of silver. Later he tried to return the money, threw it into the temple, and hanged himself. The priests used the silver to buy a potter's field as a graveyard for foreigners — Akeldama, the Field of Blood.

question: The Roman governor Pontius Pilate, finding no fault in Jesus, washed his hands in front of the crowd and handed Jesus over to be crucified. On what hill was Jesus crucified?
context: Golgotha is Aramaic; the Latin equivalent is Calvaria, from which we get Calvary. Two thieves were crucified beside Jesus. Pilate had a sign nailed to the cross reading 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews' in three languages.

question: On Easter morning, women came to anoint Jesus's body with spices. They found the great stone rolled away and the tomb empty. What did the angel inside tell them?
answer: He is risen, he is not here
choices: He is risen, he is not here
The Romans have taken his body
Wait here until the disciples come
Anoint the stones for his coming
context: The Gospels record slightly different details — the women included Mary Magdalene. The risen Jesus appeared first to her in the garden. She did not recognize him at first; she thought he was the gardener until he said her name.

question: After his resurrection, Jesus appeared to his disciples many times over forty days. Then on the Mount of Olives, in their sight, something happened. What?
answer: He ascended into heaven on a cloud
choices: He ascended into heaven on a cloud
He vanished into a pillar of fire
He walked away east of the Jordan
He sailed across the Sea of Galilee
context: The Ascension is in Acts 1. Two angels in white told the staring disciples: 'This same Jesus shall come again in like manner as ye have seen him go.' Christians celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter.

question: Fifty days after Easter, the disciples were gathered in Jerusalem when a sound like wind filled the house and tongues of flame appeared above their heads. They poured into the street preaching. What is this day called?
context: The story is in Acts 2. Pentecost is the traditional birthday of the Christian Church. About three thousand were baptized that day. Peter preached the first Christian sermon to pilgrims from across the Roman world.

question: An old bishop of Smyrna was ordered by the Roman proconsul to curse Christ or burn at the stake. He was 86 years old. He refused, saying he had served Christ all his life. Who was he?
context: The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* (c. 156 AD) is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyr's death outside the New Testament. Witnesses said the flames bent away from him, so a soldier finally stabbed him with a sword.

question: A Roman soldier and secret Christian was discovered by Emperor Diocletian and tied to a tree to be killed by his fellow archers. He survived the arrows and was later clubbed to death. Who was he?
context: Sebastian is one of the most-painted saints in Western art — the arrow-pierced young man tied to a tree or post. He was nursed back to health after the arrows by the widow Irene, returned to confront Diocletian, and was then clubbed.

question: A Roman deacon was roasted alive on a gridiron in 258 AD. Tradition says he joked to his torturers: 'Turn me over — I am done on this side.' Who was he?
context: Lawrence was the treasurer of the Roman church. When ordered to hand over the church's wealth, he gathered the poor and showed them to the prefect, saying these were the church's treasures. He is now the patron saint of cooks and comedians.

question: A young missionary bishop returned to fifth-century Ireland and is traditionally credited with driving every snake on the island into the sea. He also used a three-leaf shamrock to explain the Trinity. Who was he?
context: Patrick was kidnapped as a Romano-British teenager by Irish raiders and enslaved as a shepherd before escaping. He felt called to return as a missionary. Ireland has no native snakes — possibly because of glacial geology, but the legend remains.

question: A Roman soldier and Christian saint is famous in legend for slaying a dragon to rescue a princess. He became the patron saint of England and his red cross on white appears on the English flag. Who was he?
context: George was a Roman officer martyred under Diocletian around 303 AD for refusing to recant his Christian faith. The dragon legend grew in the medieval Golden Legend. The English Crusaders adopted his red cross as their battle banner.

question: A young noble in Assisi gave up his rich father's wealth, stripped naked in the town square, and embraced a life of total poverty. He preached even to the birds. Who was he?
context: Francis of Assisi (1181-1226) founded the Franciscan order. He received the stigmata — Christ's wounds — on Mount La Verna. He composed the *Canticle of the Sun*. He is the patron saint of animals and ecology.

question: A teenage peasant girl heard voices from saints telling her to lead France against the English. She put on armor, broke the siege of Orleans at 17, and was burned at the stake at 19. Who was she?
context: Joan said the voices were Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret. She crowned Charles VII at Reims in 1429. The English captured her, tried her as a heretic in Rouen, and burned her on May 30, 1431. She was canonized in 1920.

question: A young deacon was the first Christian killed for his faith. Stoned outside Jerusalem, he saw a vision of Jesus in heaven before he died. A young Pharisee named Saul watched the cloaks of the killers. Who was the deacon?
context: Stephen's story is in Acts 6-7. As he died he prayed 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — echoing Christ's words from the cross. The Saul who held the cloaks would soon become the Apostle Paul.

question: A Pharisee from Tarsus was traveling to Damascus to arrest Christians when a blinding light struck him from heaven and a voice asked: 'Why do you persecute me?' He was renamed Paul. What had he been called before?
context: The story is in Acts 9. Saul was blind for three days until a Christian named Ananias healed him. Paul wrote thirteen letters of the New Testament and was eventually beheaded in Rome under Emperor Nero.

question: On the island of Patmos, an elderly apostle exiled by Roman authorities had a vision of heaven and the end of the world. He wrote it down as the final book of the Bible. Who was the apostle?
context: John was one of the original twelve apostles, the 'beloved disciple,' and tradition holds he was the only one not martyred. His vision is the Book of Revelation. He had also written the fourth Gospel and three letters.

question: In the Garden of Eden, a serpent told the first woman that if she ate from the forbidden tree she would not die — instead she would become like God, knowing good and evil. Eve ate, and gave the fruit to Adam. Their eyes were opened and they hid in shame. When God walked in the garden in the cool of the day, what was their punishment?
answer: Banishment from Eden and a life of toil and death
choices: Banishment from Eden and a life of toil and death
Seven days of darkness without food
A flood that drowned the garden forever
An angel killed the serpent in their sight
context: The story is in Genesis 3. God placed cherubim with a flaming sword east of Eden to guard the way back to the tree of life. The expulsion is sometimes called the Fall — humanity's separation from its original innocence.

question: Two brothers — sons of Adam and Eve — brought offerings to God. Cain brought crops from his fields; Abel brought the firstborn of his flock. God favored Abel's lamb but not Cain's grain. Cain's face fell with jealousy. He invited Abel into a field and killed him there. When God asked Cain where his brother was, what did Cain reply?
choices: I have not seen him since the dawn
He has gone to tend the flock at the spring
I am only a tiller of soil, not a watchman
context: The story is in Genesis 4. God placed a mark on Cain so no one would kill him, exiled him east of Eden to the land of Nod, and made him a wanderer. The first murder in scripture was also the first instance of fratricide — brother against brother.

question: God warned Noah that a flood would destroy the wicked earth and told him to build an ark of gopher wood, 300 cubits long, with three decks. Noah took his wife, three sons and their wives, and a pair of every kind of animal aboard. The rain fell forty days and forty nights. When the ark finally came to rest, on what mountain did it land?
context: The story is in Genesis 8. Mount Ararat is in eastern Turkey, near the borders of Iran and Armenia. After the flood, God set a rainbow in the sky as a sign of his promise never to destroy the earth by water again.

question: After the flood, all people on earth spoke one language. They gathered on a plain in Shinar and began building a great tower meant to reach the heavens — both to make a name for themselves and to keep from being scattered. God came down, saw their pride, and confused their language so they could no longer understand each other. The work stopped and they scattered. By what name is the unfinished tower known?
context: The story is in Genesis 11. Babel sounds like the Hebrew word for 'confused.' The name is also the root of 'Babylon.' The scattering at Babel explains the origin of the world's many languages and is mirrored, in reverse, at Pentecost in Acts 2.

question: God called an old man in Ur of the Chaldeans to leave his country, his kindred, and his father's house, and travel to a land God would show him. The man was 75 and his wife Sarah could not have children. God still promised him a son and descendants more numerous than the stars. The man went. By what name is he now known?
context: The story is in Genesis 12. His original name was Abram; God renamed him Abraham, meaning 'father of many nations.' He is called the father of three world faiths — Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Sarah bore Isaac when she was 90 and Abraham was 100.

question: God tested Abraham's faith by ordering him to take his only son Isaac, climb a mountain in the land of Moriah, and offer him as a burnt sacrifice. Abraham bound the boy on the altar of stones and raised the knife. At that moment an angel of the Lord called out and stopped him. Abraham looked up and saw something caught in a nearby thicket. What was provided as the sacrifice instead?
answer: A ram caught by its horns
choices: A ram caught by its horns
A dove sent down from heaven
A lamb laid at the altar
A lion lying down beside it
context: The story is in Genesis 22. Christians have long read the binding of Isaac (the *Akedah*) as a foreshadowing of God offering His own Son on the cross. The same hill in Jerusalem traditionally is said to be both Moriah and Golgotha.

question: Two cities of the plain became so wicked that God sent two angels to inspect them and warn the one righteous man — Lot — to flee with his family. The angels told them: do not stop, do not look back. Fire and sulfur rained down. Lot's wife glanced back at the burning city and was instantly turned into a pillar of salt. What were the two destroyed cities?
context: The story is in Genesis 19. Abraham had begged God to spare the cities for the sake of ten righteous men. Not even ten could be found. A salt formation by the Dead Sea — near where the cities are thought to have stood — is still called 'Lot's Wife' by locals.

question: Isaac's twin sons Esau and Jacob struggled even in the womb. Esau was born first, red and hairy, and grew up a hunter; Jacob was a quiet shepherd. When their father Isaac was old and blind, Jacob disguised himself with goat skins on his arms to feel like his hairy brother and tricked his father into giving him the blessing meant for the firstborn. What did Esau sell his birthright for earlier?
answer: A bowl of red lentil stew
choices: A bowl of red lentil stew
A purse of forty silver shekels
context: The story is in Genesis 25 and 27. Esau came home famished from a hunt and Jacob made him swear away his birthright before feeding him. The name Edom — Esau's later name — comes from the same root as 'red,' for the stew.

question: Jacob's twelve sons grew jealous of their brother Joseph because their father gave him a coat of many colors. They threw him into a pit, then sold him to traders bound for Egypt for twenty pieces of silver, dipping his coat in goat blood to fool their father. Years later, famine drove them to Egypt to beg for grain. Who did they unknowingly face?
answer: Joseph, now second in Egypt only to Pharaoh
choices: Joseph, now second in Egypt only to Pharaoh
An Egyptian priest who recognized them
A desert chieftain of a Bedouin tribe
context: The story is in Genesis 37-45. Joseph had risen to power by interpreting Pharaoh's dreams of seven fat cows and seven thin cows — seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine. He forgave his brothers and moved the whole family to Egypt to save them.

question: In prison, Joseph interpreted dreams for Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker — foretelling the cupbearer's restoration and the baker's hanging. Both came true. Two years later Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones. No Egyptian wise man could explain it. The cupbearer remembered Joseph. What was Joseph's interpretation?
answer: Seven years of plenty, then seven of famine
choices: Seven years of plenty, then seven of famine
Three generations of war with Hittites
A plague that would empty the river Nile
Birth of a prince who would rule Egypt
context: The story is in Genesis 41. Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin cows, and seven full ears of grain swallowed by seven withered ones. Joseph advised Pharaoh to store one-fifth of every harvest during the years of plenty. Pharaoh made Joseph second only to himself.

question: An Egyptian princess discovered a Hebrew baby floating in a basket of pitch among the reeds of the Nile and raised him as her own son in Pharaoh's palace. As a young man he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew slave and fled to Midian, where he tended his father-in-law Jethro's flocks. Years later he saw a bush on fire that did not burn up, and God called him from the bush. Who was he?
context: The story is in Exodus 1-3. Moses's mother had hidden him in the basket to save him from Pharaoh's order to kill every Hebrew baby boy. His sister Miriam watched the basket; the princess hired Miriam's mother as the baby's nurse. Moses became the prophet who led Israel out of slavery.

question: When Pharaoh refused to let the Hebrew slaves go, God sent ten plagues on Egypt — the Nile to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, livestock disease, boils, hail with fire, locusts, three days of darkness, and finally the death of every firstborn son. The Hebrews were spared the last plague by marking their doorposts. With what blood?
answer: The blood of a Passover lamb
choices: The blood of a Passover lamb
The blood of a red bull
Their own blood from a cut
context: The story is in Exodus 7-12. The angel of death passed over the marked houses — the origin of Passover. Pharaoh's own firstborn son died. Pharaoh let the Hebrews go that very night. Christians see the lamb's blood as a foreshadowing of Christ, 'the Lamb of God.'

question: Pharaoh sent six hundred chariots after the freed Hebrews. They reached the Red Sea with no way out. Moses lifted his staff and a strong east wind blew all night, parting the sea into walls of water on each side. The Hebrews crossed on dry ground. What happened when the Egyptian army followed?
answer: The waters crashed back and drowned them all
choices: The waters crashed back and drowned them all
The Egyptians turned back to Egypt in terror
An angel struck them blind on the seabed
Lightning destroyed their chariots from above
context: The story is in Exodus 14. Moses's sister Miriam led the women in a song of victory with tambourines: 'Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.' This is one of the oldest songs in the Bible.

question: In the wilderness the Hebrews grumbled that they had no food. God sent quail in the evenings and in the mornings a strange flaky white substance appeared on the ground with the dew. The people gathered it daily and ate it for the forty years they wandered. They called it by a name meaning 'What is it?' What was the bread from heaven called?
context: The story is in Exodus 16. The people gathered an omer per person each day. On the sixth day they gathered double so they could rest on the Sabbath. The manna stopped when they entered the Promised Land and ate its produce. Jesus called himself the true bread from heaven (John 6).

question: After leading the Hebrews out of Egypt, Moses climbed Mount Sinai. For forty days the mountain was wrapped in thick cloud, fire, and the sound of a trumpet, while the people watched from below in terror. God gave Moses two stone tablets carved by God himself, containing the law that would govern Israel. What are these laws called?
context: The story is in Exodus 19-20 and Deuteronomy 5. The first commandments cover duties to God; the rest, duties to neighbor. When Moses came down and saw the people worshipping a golden calf, he smashed the tablets in rage. God gave him a second set to replace them, which Israel kept in the Ark of the Covenant.

question: While Moses was on Sinai receiving the Law, the Hebrews grew impatient. They asked Moses's brother Aaron to make them a god they could see. Aaron collected their gold earrings, melted them down, and shaped them into an idol they then worshipped with feasting and dancing. What animal-shape idol did they make?
context: The story is in Exodus 32. Moses came down the mountain, smashed the tablets, ground the calf to powder, mixed it in water, and made the people drink it. Three thousand were killed for the idolatry. Aaron blamed the people: 'I cast the gold into the fire, and out came this calf.'

question: When the Hebrew spies returned from Canaan with news of giants in the land, the people lost heart and refused to enter. As punishment they wandered the wilderness forty years until that whole generation died. Only two of the original spies — who had urged faith — lived to enter the Promised Land. One was Joshua. Who was the other?
context: The story is in Numbers 13-14. Joshua and Caleb had said: 'We are well able to overcome it; the Lord is with us.' The other ten spies had spread fear about the giants of Anak. Forty years later, Joshua led the people into Canaan and Caleb, now 85, asked for the hill country of Hebron and conquered it.

question: Moses led the Hebrews for forty years through the wilderness but never entered the Promised Land himself — God told him he would only see it from a mountain. He climbed Mount Nebo, looked across the Jordan into Canaan, and died there at 120 years old. His body was buried by God in a hidden grave that no one ever found. Who took over as leader of Israel?
context: The story is in Deuteronomy 34. Joshua had been Moses's assistant for decades. His name in Hebrew is the same as 'Jesus' — meaning 'the Lord saves.' Joshua led the Hebrews across the Jordan on dry ground, just as Moses had led them across the Red Sea.

question: When Joshua brought the Hebrews into Canaan, the first city they faced was Jericho, with its massive walls. God's instruction was strange — for six days they were to march around the city once a day in silence, with the Ark and seven priests blowing rams' horns. On the seventh day, they marched seven times. Then what?
answer: The priests blew a long blast and the walls fell flat
choices: The priests blew a long blast and the walls fell flat
Angels descended and opened the city gates
The defenders fled in confusion at dawn
Lightning split the walls in three places
context: The story is in Joshua 6. The Hebrews then took the city, sparing only Rahab — a woman who had hidden Israelite spies in her house, marked by a scarlet cord in her window. Modern archaeology at Jericho has shown that the ancient walls did collapse outward, contrary to ordinary siege patterns.

question: An Israelite judge named Samson had supernatural strength as long as his hair was never cut — part of his Nazirite vow. He tore a lion apart with his bare hands, killed a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, and burned their crops by tying torches to the tails of three hundred foxes. His weakness was women. Who finally tricked him into revealing the secret of his strength?
context: The story is in Judges 13-16. The Philistines paid Delilah 1,100 pieces of silver each. After she cut his hair, they gouged out his eyes and set him to grind grain in prison. At a Philistine festival in the temple of Dagon his hair had grown back. He pulled down the pillars, killing himself and three thousand Philistines.

question: An Israelite woman of Bethlehem named Naomi lost her husband and both her sons in Moab. She told her two daughters-in-law to return to their own people. One did. The other refused, saying: 'Whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.' She followed Naomi back to Bethlehem and gleaned in the fields of a kinsman who married her. Who was she?
context: The story is in the Book of Ruth. The kinsman was Boaz. Their great-grandson was King David. Ruth, a Moabite by birth, is one of only five women named in Jesus's genealogy in Matthew 1 — a foreigner brought into the line of the Messiah.

question: A Jewish orphan named Esther was raised by her cousin Mordecai and chosen as queen of Persia by King Ahasuerus. The king's minister Haman built a fifty-cubit gallows to hang Mordecai and tricked the king into signing a decree to kill all Jews. Esther risked death by going uninvited to the king and exposed Haman at a banquet. What was Haman's fate?
choices: Crushed by his own house's stones
context: The story is in the Book of Esther. The festival of Purim — celebrated by Jews each spring with costumes, gifts, and noisemakers at the mention of Haman's name — commemorates the deliverance. Esther is one of two books in the Bible (Song of Songs is the other) that never mentions God by name.

question: A nine-foot Philistine giant named Goliath stood in the Valley of Elah for forty days, daring Israel to send one warrior. The shepherd boy David, bringing food to his brothers, heard the giant's mockery. He refused armor, took his sling and five smooth stones, and ran at Goliath. After the stone struck, what did David do?
answer: Cut off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword
choices: Cut off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword
Tied him with cord and dragged him to Saul
Pierced him with an Israelite soldier's spear
Let the Philistines carry away their champion
context: The story is in 1 Samuel 17. David then carried the head back to King Saul. The Philistine army fled when they saw their champion dead. David later became Israel's greatest king and ancestor of Jesus, and the slaying of Goliath is one of the most-painted scenes in Western art.

question: King David, walking on his palace roof, saw a beautiful woman bathing. She was Bathsheba, wife of David's loyal soldier Uriah the Hittite. David sent for her and slept with her. When she became pregnant, David had Uriah placed in the front line of battle to die. The prophet Nathan came to David with what?
answer: A parable: a rich man who stole a poor man's lamb
choices: A parable: a rich man who stole a poor man's lamb
A scroll of all Israelite sins since the Exodus
A vision of David's palace burning to the ground
A direct accusation naming both David and Uriah
context: The story is in 2 Samuel 11-12. David, listening to the parable, raged that the rich man deserved to die. Nathan answered: 'Thou art the man.' David repented. The baby died. Bathsheba's next son with David was Solomon, who would build the Temple. Psalm 51 — David's confession — comes from this episode.

question: When King Solomon was a young king at Gibeon, God appeared to him in a dream and offered him anything he asked. Solomon did not ask for long life or wealth or victory over enemies. He asked instead for one specific gift — and God was so pleased that He gave Solomon riches and honor as well. What did Solomon ask for?
answer: Wisdom to govern God's people well
choices: Wisdom to govern God's people well
Strength to defeat all the surrounding kings
Knowledge of every secret in heaven
A son who would rule a thousand years
context: The story is in 1 Kings 3. Soon afterward two women came to Solomon claiming the same baby. He ordered the baby cut in half — knowing the true mother would beg him to spare the child even if she lost it. She did, and Solomon gave her the child. All Israel heard the verdict and stood in awe.

question: Ahab and Jezebel had promoted Baal worship in Israel. The prophet Elijah challenged Baal's 450 prophets on Mount Carmel — each side build an altar and call down fire. The Baal prophets cried and cut themselves all morning; nothing came. Elijah soaked his altar with twelve barrels of water and prayed. What did God do?
answer: Fire fell and consumed altar, water, and stones
choices: Fire fell and consumed altar, water, and stones
An angel appeared and threw down Baal's priests
The skies opened and rain ended the drought
A whirlwind carried Elijah up before the priests
context: The story is in 1 Kings 18. After the fire, Elijah had all 450 prophets of Baal slaughtered at the Kishon brook. Queen Jezebel swore to kill Elijah; he fled to Mount Horeb (Sinai), where God spoke to him not in wind or fire but in a 'still small voice.'

question: King Darius signed a decree that anyone praying to any god but the king for thirty days would be thrown to the lions. The Hebrew official Daniel kept praying three times a day with his window open toward Jerusalem. Reported by jealous rivals, he was thrown into the den. At dawn the king called out and Daniel answered alive. Why?
answer: An angel had shut the lions' mouths
choices: An angel had shut the lions' mouths
Daniel had hid in a side tunnel all night
The lions had been drugged by a guard
Daniel had tamed them with psalms
context: The story is in Daniel 6. Darius then threw the conspiring officials AND their families into the same den, and the lions devoured them before they hit the floor. Darius issued a new decree honoring Daniel's God. Daniel later had visions of four beasts and of an end-time figure called 'the Ancient of Days.'

question: God told the prophet Jonah to go to wicked Nineveh and preach repentance. Jonah disobeyed and boarded a ship sailing the opposite way, to Tarshish. A storm arose. The sailors cast lots; the lot fell on Jonah. He confessed and told them to throw him overboard. They did, and the sea grew calm. What then happened to Jonah?
answer: A great fish swallowed him whole for three days
choices: A great fish swallowed him whole for three days
He swam back to shore on a piece of cargo
Angels lifted him out of the water at dawn
He drowned and was raised on the third day
context: The story is in the Book of Jonah. The fish spat him out on dry land. Jonah then went to Nineveh and preached; the whole city repented in sackcloth and ashes — even the cattle. Jesus referred to 'the sign of Jonah' to point ahead to his own three days in the tomb.

question: Job, a righteous wealthy man, had seven sons, three daughters, and great flocks. In one day raiders killed his servants, fire burned his sheep, raiders took his camels, and a wind crushed the house on all ten children. Boils struck him head to toe. His wife told him to curse God. What did Job say?
answer: The Lord gave and has taken away; blessed be his name
choices: The Lord gave and has taken away; blessed be his name
Why has God forgotten me when my faith was strong?
I will trust no god who allows such evil to fall
Let me die at once and end this useless suffering
context: The story is in the Book of Job. Three friends came to comfort him and instead lectured him about his hidden sins. God finally answered Job out of a whirlwind with a series of awesome questions about creation. In the end, God restored Job double — fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, and ten more children.

question: In Nazareth, the angel Gabriel appeared to a young woman engaged to a carpenter named Joseph. He told her she would conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son named Jesus, who would be called the Son of God and inherit the throne of David. Her answer became one of the most-quoted lines in Christianity. What did she say?
answer: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me
choices: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me
Who am I that the Lord should send his angel?
I am not worthy that such a child be given me
Let it not be, for I am not yet wed to Joseph
context: The story is in Luke 1. Mary's response is called her Fiat — Latin for 'let it be done.' The visit is called the Annunciation, celebrated by Christians on March 25. Painters from Fra Angelico to Botticelli have made the Annunciation one of the most depicted scenes in Western art.

question: Caesar Augustus decreed a census of the Roman world. Joseph traveled from Nazareth to Bethlehem with his pregnant wife Mary. The inn was full. Mary gave birth where animals were kept and laid the baby in a feeding trough. That night an angel appeared to shepherds in nearby fields. What did the angel say?
answer: Unto you is born this day a Savior, Christ the Lord
choices: Unto you is born this day a Savior, Christ the Lord
The temple in Jerusalem will fall before morning
The Romans will soon flee the holy land in fear
Caesar is dead and a new emperor shall rise
context: The story is in Luke 2. Suddenly a multitude of the heavenly host appeared, praising God: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.' The shepherds left their flocks at once and found the baby in the manger, as the angel had said.

question: Wise men from the East followed a star to Jerusalem, asking where the newborn 'king of the Jews' was to be found. The current king — Herod the Great — was alarmed. He gathered his scholars, who pointed to the prophet Micah's prediction of Bethlehem. Herod told the wise men to bring news back when they found the child, secretly meaning to kill him. The wise men brought three gifts. Name one besides gold.
context: The story is in Matthew 2. The wise men, warned in a dream, went home another way. The traditional names — Caspar, Melchior, Balthazar — are not in the Gospel. Gold honored a king, frankincense (used in temple worship) honored a priest, and myrrh — a burial spice — foreshadowed Jesus's death.

question: When the wise men did not return to Herod the Great as promised, the king flew into a rage. To kill any future rival, he ordered every male child under age two in Bethlehem killed. An angel warned Joseph in a dream to flee in the night with Mary and Jesus. To what country did the Holy Family escape?
context: The story is in Matthew 2. The killing is called the Massacre of the Innocents. The Holy Family stayed in Egypt until Herod died, then returned to Nazareth. Matthew links the flight to Hosea's prophecy: 'Out of Egypt have I called my son.' The Flight into Egypt is the subject of countless medieval paintings.

question: Jesus's cousin John lived as a hermit — clothed in camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, baptizing people in the Jordan. He warned: 'I baptize with water, but one is coming whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.' When Jesus himself came to be baptized, what happened as he came up from the water?
answer: The heavens opened and a voice said: This is my beloved Son
choices: The heavens opened and a voice said: This is my beloved Son
John fell to his knees on the muddy river bank
Twelve doves descended on the Jordan together
A burning column appeared above the river bed
context: The story is in Matthew 3. The Spirit descended on Jesus like a dove. This Baptism of the Lord opens his public ministry. John would later be beheaded by Herod Antipas — his head served on a platter at Herodias's daughter's request after she danced for the king at his birthday feast.

question: Jesus walked along the Sea of Galilee and saw two brothers — Simon and Andrew — casting nets. He said: 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.' They left their nets at once. Farther on he saw two more brothers, James and John, mending nets with their father Zebedee. They left their boat and followed too. What did Jesus rename Simon?
context: The story is in Matthew 4 and 16. Jesus later said to him: 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.' Peter became the chief apostle. He would also deny Jesus three times before the cock crowed on the night of the arrest, and weep bitterly.

question: At a wedding in Cana of Galilee, the wine ran out. Mary turned to her son and quietly said: 'They have no wine.' Jesus told the servants to fill six stone water jars to the brim — each holding 20 to 30 gallons — and to draw some out and take it to the steward. The steward, not knowing where it came from, called the bridegroom and praised him for what?
answer: Keeping the best wine for last
choices: Keeping the best wine for last
Watering wine for the long evening
Mixing honey in for the sweetness
context: The story is in John 2. This was Jesus's first public miracle and the beginning of his ministry. The custom was to serve the best wine first; the steward marveled that the bridegroom had reversed it. The six jars held 120 to 180 gallons of wine — far more than any wedding feast would need.

question: A crowd of five thousand men, plus women and children, followed Jesus into a remote place in Galilee. As evening came, the disciples wanted to send the people away to find food. Jesus told them to feed the crowd. They had nothing except what a small boy had brought. Jesus took it, looked up to heaven, blessed it, broke it, and distributed it. What did the boy have?
answer: Five barley loaves and two small fish
choices: Five barley loaves and two small fish
Three round cakes and a jar of honey
A wineskin and a basket of dates
Twelve fig cakes and dried lamb
context: The story is in all four Gospels — the only miracle besides the Resurrection recorded by every Gospel writer. Everyone ate and was satisfied. Twelve baskets of leftover scraps were gathered, one for each apostle. The next day the crowd searched for Jesus across the lake; he told them: 'I am the bread of life.'

question: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus sent his disciples ahead in a boat while he stayed on the mountain to pray. A storm rose in the night and they strained at the oars. In the fourth watch they saw a figure walking toward them across the water. They cried out, thinking it was a ghost. Then they heard Jesus's voice. What did Peter ask?
answer: If it is you, Lord, bid me come on the water
choices: If it is you, Lord, bid me come on the water
Master, why have you left us alone so long?
Lord, calm this storm before we all drown
Bid an angel come and steer our boat
context: The story is in Matthew 14. Peter walked on the water toward Jesus but, seeing the wind, began to sink. Jesus reached out his hand and caught him: 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' When they climbed into the boat the wind ceased. The disciples worshipped him: 'Truly thou art the Son of God.'

question: Jesus's friend Lazarus of Bethany had died. By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. His sister Martha said: 'Lord, by this time he stinketh.' Jesus had the stone rolled away. He prayed aloud so the crowd would believe, then cried with a loud voice into the tomb. What did Jesus say?
choices: Rise up, my friend, and come to me
Wake from sleep, you whom I love
Loose his bands and let him go
context: The story is in John 11. Lazarus came out still wrapped in grave-cloths. Jesus said: 'Loose him, and let him go.' Just before raising Lazarus, Jesus had wept — the shortest verse in the Bible: 'Jesus wept.' Many who saw the miracle believed; others reported it to the chief priests, who plotted his death.

question: A lawyer asked Jesus: 'And who is my neighbor?' Jesus answered with a story. A traveler was robbed and beaten on the road to Jericho. A priest passed by on the other side. A Levite did the same. Then an unexpected traveler — from a people the Jews despised — stopped, bandaged the wounds, brought the man to an inn, and paid for his care. Who was that traveler?
context: The story is in Luke 10. Jesus then asked: 'Which of these three was a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' The lawyer answered: 'He that showed mercy.' Jesus said: 'Go, and do thou likewise.' The parable's hero is a member of a hated group — making mercy the test of true neighborhood.

question: A man had two sons. The younger demanded his inheritance, traveled to a far country, and squandered it on wild living. When famine came he hired himself out to feed pigs — and was so hungry he longed to eat their food. He decided to return home and become a servant. While he was still a long way off, what did the father do?
answer: Ran to him, embraced him, and threw a feast
choices: Ran to him, embraced him, and threw a feast
Sent servants to bind him in the field
Made him work years to earn forgiveness
Refused to see him until he gave account
context: The story is in Luke 15 — the parable of the Prodigal Son, the most famous of Jesus's parables. The father killed the fatted calf and put a ring on the son's hand and shoes on his feet. The elder brother, who had stayed and worked, resented the welcome. Jesus told the parable to show how God receives sinners who return.

question: Jesus told the parable of a shepherd with a hundred sheep. One wandered off. The shepherd left the ninety-nine in the open country and searched until he found the lost one. He carried it home on his shoulders, then called his neighbors together to celebrate. Jesus drew a parallel — what does this picture in heaven?
answer: Joy in heaven over one sinner who repents
choices: Joy in heaven over one sinner who repents
The shepherds of Israel who lost their flocks
The chosen few who matter more than crowds
How God's love divides the worthy from the rest
context: The parable is in Luke 15 and Matthew 18. It precedes the Lost Coin and the Prodigal Son in Luke — three parables on the same theme. The image of Jesus as the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep also runs through John 10. Early Christians often pictured Christ as a shepherd carrying a lamb on his shoulders.

question: Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to the smallest of all garden seeds. When planted, it grows into a great plant — a kind of tree — so large that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches. He used this image to show that the kingdom starts almost invisibly and grows beyond expectation. What seed?
context: The parable is in Matthew 13, Mark 4, and Luke 13. Jesus also said that faith as small as a mustard seed could move mountains. The actual black mustard plant of the Holy Land can grow up to ten feet — a tree from a tiny seed. The parable is paired with the parable of the leaven hidden in three measures of flour.

question: On a mountainside in Galilee, Jesus preached his most famous sermon. It opens with eight blessings: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit ... Blessed are they that mourn ... Blessed are the meek ... Blessed are the pure in heart ...' Each line begins with the same word. What are these blessings called as a group?
context: The Sermon on the Mount is in Matthew 5-7. Beyond the Beatitudes it contains the Lord's Prayer, the Golden Rule ('do unto others as you would have them do unto you'), and the command to love your enemies. Augustine called it 'the perfect standard of the Christian life.' Tolstoy considered it the heart of Christianity.

question: On the night before his crucifixion, Jesus gathered the twelve disciples in an upper room in Jerusalem for the Passover meal. He took bread, broke it, and said: 'This is my body, given for you.' He took the cup of wine and said: 'This is my blood of the new covenant.' During the meal he announced that one of them at the table would betray him. Who slipped out into the night?
context: The story is in all four Gospels — the Last Supper. The disciples had asked: 'Surely not I, Lord?' Judas led the temple guards to the Garden of Gethsemane and identified Jesus with a kiss for thirty pieces of silver. Christians celebrate this meal as the Eucharist or Holy Communion.

question: After the Last Supper, Jesus and the disciples went to a garden on the Mount of Olives. Jesus prayed in agony, sweating drops like blood: 'Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.' The disciples slept while he prayed. Then Judas arrived with armed men. What was the name of the garden?
context: Gethsemane means 'oil press' in Aramaic. The garden was at the foot of the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. Some olive trees there are thought to be over two thousand years old. Peter drew his sword and cut off the high priest's servant's ear; Jesus healed it and rebuked Peter — 'Put up thy sword.'

question: Peter swore at the Last Supper that he would never deny Jesus, even if all others did. Jesus answered: 'Before the cock crows twice, thou shalt deny me three times.' In the courtyard while Jesus was tried, a servant girl recognized Peter. He denied it twice. The third time he cursed and swore he did not know the man. Then what happened?
answer: The cock crowed and Peter wept bitterly
choices: The cock crowed and Peter wept bitterly
The temple guards seized Peter at once
Jesus called across to forgive him there
Peter ran to John to confess his sin
context: The story is in all four Gospels. Luke adds the detail that 'the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.' After the Resurrection, Jesus three times asked Peter: 'Do you love me?' — once for each denial — and entrusted him with: 'Feed my sheep.' Peter became the chief apostle of the early Church.

question: The Roman governor Pilate examined Jesus and found no fault. He hoped to release him by offering the crowd a choice between Jesus and the bandit Barabbas. Stirred by the priests, the crowd demanded Barabbas. Pilate asked: 'What shall I do with Jesus?' The crowd cried: 'Crucify him.' What did Pilate do then?
answer: Washed his hands publicly and handed Jesus over
choices: Washed his hands publicly and handed Jesus over
Refused and sent Jesus back to Herod for trial
Released both prisoners against the crowd's will
Took Jesus into his palace to hide him from harm
context: The story is in Matthew 27. Pilate said: 'I am innocent of this man's blood.' The crowd answered: 'His blood be on us and on our children.' Jesus was scourged, mocked with a crown of thorns and a purple robe, and led to Golgotha. A sign was nailed above the cross: 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,' in three languages.

question: Early on Sunday morning, women came to Jesus's tomb with spices to anoint his body. They wondered who would roll away the heavy stone. When they arrived, the stone was already rolled away. The tomb was empty. An angel in shining clothes sat inside and spoke to them. What did the angel say?
answer: He is not here; he is risen, as he said
choices: He is not here; he is risen, as he said
Wait here for his disciples in the city
The Romans have taken his body away
Anoint the linen cloths he has left behind
context: The story is in all four Gospels. The women included Mary Magdalene. The risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene in the garden. She did not recognize him at first — she thought he was the gardener until he said her name. He told her: 'Go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father and your Father.'

question: In 155 AD the bishop Polycarp of Smyrna, once taught by the apostle John, was dragged to the arena. The proconsul ordered him to curse Christ. Polycarp, then 86, answered: 'Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He never did me wrong. How can I now blaspheme my King who saved me?' What was his fate?
answer: Burned at the stake, then stabbed when flames bent away
choices: Burned at the stake, then stabbed when flames bent away
Beheaded with a sword in the public square at noon
Thrown to the lions in the great arena of Smyrna
Stoned by the crowd outside the proconsul's villa
context: The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* (c. 156 AD) is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyr's death outside the New Testament. Witnesses said the flames formed a vault around Polycarp without touching him. A soldier finally pierced him with a sword, and a dove was said to fly up from the wound.

question: Sebastian, a young officer of the Praetorian Guard, was found to be a secret Christian under Emperor Diocletian around 286 AD. Diocletian had him tied to a tree and shot full of arrows by his fellow archers. They left him for dead, but the widow Irene found him alive and nursed him to health. He returned to confront Diocletian. What was his second fate?
answer: Clubbed to death by Diocletian's order
choices: Clubbed to death by Diocletian's order
Beheaded by sword on the city wall
Burned at the stake outside the gate
Strangled in his cell that same night
context: Saint Sebastian became one of the most-painted saints in Western art — the arrow-pierced young man tied to a tree or post. He is patron of soldiers, athletes, and plague sufferers (the arrows of disease). His relics are kept in the basilica of San Sebastiano on the Appian Way in Rome.

question: In 258 AD, the Roman prefect demanded the church's treasures from the Roman deacon Lawrence. Lawrence asked three days, gathered the poor, sick, and disabled of the city, and presented them: 'These are the treasures of the church.' Enraged, the prefect roasted him alive over a gridiron. What did tradition say Lawrence joked as he died?
answer: Turn me over, for I am done on this side
choices: Turn me over, for I am done on this side
Let me burn for the souls of my flock
Caesar may take my flesh but not my Lord
I die for Christ and rise to crown him King
context: Lawrence (San Lorenzo) is one of the most-honored martyrs in Rome. The Escorial palace in Spain is built in the shape of a gridiron in his honor — Philip II's victory at the Battle of Saint-Quentin in 1557 had fallen on Lawrence's feast day, August 10. Lawrence became the patron saint of cooks and comedians.

question: A Romano-British teenager was kidnapped by Irish raiders at sixteen and enslaved as a shepherd in Ireland for six years before escaping by walking two hundred miles to a ship. Years later, after becoming a bishop, he felt a calling in a dream and returned to Ireland — to the very people who had enslaved him — as a missionary. Tradition credits him with driving every snake on the island into the sea. Who was he?
context: Patrick used the three-leaf shamrock to explain the Trinity. His *Confessio* — the story of his enslavement and conversion — is one of the few surviving documents from fifth-century Britain. Ireland has no native snakes, possibly because of glacial geology, but the legend remains. His feast day, March 17, is celebrated worldwide.

question: A Roman soldier and saint, executed around 303 AD under Diocletian for refusing to renounce his Christian faith, became the patron of England, Catalonia, Georgia, and many other places. In medieval legend, he rescued a princess from a dragon outside the city of Silene by piercing it with his lance and binding it with her girdle. The English Crusaders carried his red cross on white as their battle banner. Who was he?
context: George was a Roman officer of Greek origin. The dragon story grew in the medieval *Golden Legend* (13th century). The English flag is his red cross on a white field — adopted as a national symbol after the Crusades. Edward III made him patron of his new Order of the Garter in 1348.

question: A young Italian nobleman in Assisi gave up his wealthy father's cloth-merchant inheritance, stripped naked in the town square before the bishop in 1206, and embraced a life of total poverty. He preached even to the birds and is said to have tamed a wolf that had been terrorizing the town of Gubbio. He received the wounds of Christ — the stigmata — on Mount La Verna. Who was he?
context: Francis (1181-1226) founded the Franciscan order of friars. He composed the *Canticle of the Sun*, addressing 'Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water.' He set up the first Nativity scene at Greccio in 1223. He is the patron saint of animals, ecology, and Italy.

question: In 1429, a 17-year-old peasant girl from Domremy arrived at the court of the uncrowned French king Charles VII. She claimed voices from Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret had told her to drive the English from France. She broke the English siege of Orleans in nine days and stood beside Charles at his coronation at Reims. Burned at age 19, who was she?
answer: Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orleans
choices: Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orleans
context: The English burned Joan as a relapsed heretic on May 30, 1431. Her last word — recorded by witnesses — was 'Jesus.' The English then threw her ashes into the Seine to deny French Catholics any relic. A retrial in 1456 declared her innocent. She was canonized as a saint in 1920.

question: After Pentecost, Jerusalem's Christians appointed seven men to serve the Greek-speaking widows. The first was Stephen, full of grace and power. False witnesses brought him before the Sanhedrin. He reviewed Israel's history, then accused his hearers of murdering 'the Righteous One.' The crowd dragged him out and stoned him. What did Stephen see as he died?
answer: Jesus standing at the right hand of God
choices: Jesus standing at the right hand of God
An angel waiting to carry him home
Twelve apostles with crowns of gold
The temple of Jerusalem turned to fire
context: Stephen's story is in Acts 6-7 — the first Christian martyr. As he died he prayed: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' and 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — echoing Christ's words from the cross. A young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus stood holding the cloaks of the killers and approving the killing. That same Saul would soon become the apostle Paul.

question: A young Pharisee from Tarsus named Saul received letters from the high priest authorizing him to arrest Christians as far away as Damascus. As he rode toward the city, a blinding light from heaven struck him down. He heard a voice say: 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?' He asked: 'Who art thou, Lord?' What was the reply?
answer: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest
choices: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest
I am the Lord God of Sinai
I am Gabriel sent from heaven
I am Christ; turn back to Jerusalem
context: The story is in Acts 9. Saul was blind for three days. A Christian named Ananias was sent by God to heal him, calling him 'Brother Saul.' Renamed Paul, he became the great apostle to the Gentiles. He would write thirteen letters of the New Testament and was eventually beheaded in Rome under Emperor Nero around 67 AD.

question: An old apostle, exiled by the Roman emperor Domitian around 95 AD to the small Aegean island of Patmos for preaching the gospel, received a vision of the end of the world while praying on a Sunday. He saw a figure of Christ amid seven golden lampstands and wrote down letters to seven churches and a long vision of the heavenly throne, the four horsemen, the dragon, the beast, and the new Jerusalem. Who was the apostle?
context: John's vision is the Book of Revelation — the final book of the Bible. John was one of the original twelve apostles, the 'beloved disciple,' and the only one tradition holds was not martyred. He had also written the fourth Gospel and three letters. He died of old age in Ephesus, the city where he had cared for Jesus's mother Mary.

question: Eight days after the Resurrection, the disciples gathered behind locked doors. The disciple Thomas — called Didymus, 'the Twin' — had not been with them at Jesus's first appearance. Thomas had refused to believe their report: 'Except I put my finger into the print of the nails, I will not believe.' Jesus appeared and offered his wounds. What did Thomas say?
choices: I see and I do believe now
context: The story is in John 20. Jesus then said: 'Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.' Tradition holds that Thomas later carried the gospel as far as India, where he founded the Mar Thoma Christian community on the Malabar Coast and was martyred at Mylapore.
